newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: U.N. condemns Tajik opposition for truce violation.
newsitem.headline: U.N. condemns Tajik opposition for truce violation.

text.p: United Nations observers in Tajikistan on Sunday condemned opposition forces for seizing a town in the north of this Central Asian state in violation of a ceasefire between the Tajik government and rebels.

The U.N. mission in Tajikistan said in a rare statement of protest that opposition forces did not allow its team to visit the town of Dzhirgatal, about 280 km (175 miles) northeast of the capital Dushanbe, which they had seized on Friday.

"The Special Representative of the U.N. Secretary-General ...sent a letter to...the leader of the united Tajik opposition today...urging strict observance of the ceasefire agreement and immediate cessation of the armed actions," the statement said.

The Tajik government and Islamic opposition groups which have waged a guerrilla war against Dushanbe authorities since their defeat in the civil war of 1992, agreed in July to extend a ceasefire signed in September 1994 in Tehran.
Each side has accused the other of frequent violations of the U.N.-brokered ceasefire, initially designed to pave the way for peace talks to try to find a compromise on political issues.
Last month, after weeks of fighting with rebels, government troops took control of the strategically important town of Tavildara, 200 km (120 miles) east of Dushanbe.
The opposition has justified its latest offensive by saying it was in response to the government attack.

President Imomali Rakhmonov, who spoke at a public meeting in Dushanbe marking five years of Tajikistan's independence, said his opponents, based mainly in Afghanistan and Iran, wanted to bring in a radical Islamic regime after communism fell.

"After the Independence Declaration, the old ideology collapsed causing a (power) vacuum and chaos in the country," Rakhmonov told a forum of Tajik diaspora attended by more than 200 people from 19 countries.
"People and political groups appeared then, who unveiled the banner of another ideology, that of religious radicalism."

Rakhmonov, Tajikistan's former communist leader, added his own vow of loyalty to Islam. "We respect the holy religion of Islam as a base of moral and spiritual cleanliness and source of culture," he said.
Tens of thousands of people have died and many more have lost their homes in fighting which has devastated the country since the former Soviet republic gained independence on September 9, 1991.
